the macrophage maturation process is impaired in malignant disease, that macrophages from patients with cancer show a defect in chemotaxis and that there is a defect in macrophage cytotoxicity in cancer.

macrophage function in cancer is disordered in a number of respects; this disorder is associated with the presence of tumour cells in the blood; and the disorder is not due to the presence of a tumour in a particular organ or to a particular tumour cell type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of mononuclear cells from peripheral blood, bone marrow and lymph node in malignant disease.
the study of the functional properties of macrophages, and the possible relationship of such functions to the host's response to malignant disease.
the role of the mononuclear phags in the defence mechanisms against malignant disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mononuclear phages are disordered in their function in neoplastic diseases.
the mononuclear phages in malignant disease are disordered in their function and maturation.

in malignant disease there is a generalised disorder in mononuclear phagetocyte function, which is most marked in the later stages of malignancy and is probably related to the degree of tumour burden.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a clear and consistent impairment of macrophage function in cancer patients, but it is not clear whether this is due to the cancer itself or to other factors such as infection or drugs.
macrophages in cancer patients are not dysfunctional.
the monocyte/macrophage system in cancer is not only dysfunctional, it is also disordered in terms of its development and maturation.
